Quick notes: Redwood prefix caching can drastically reduce token cost for Helix's chat workloads if hit rates > 30%, need to validate tenant keying to avoid leakage across customers, quantization requires cache invalidation on model-variant changes.

Transcript:
[00:00] Maya Chen: Hey everyone, thanks for joining, uh, appreciate you carving out time. Today we'll go deep on prefix or prompt caching strategy and how it plays with our runtime, batching, and the KV cache. Tomas is gonna drive the perf bits.
[00:22] Raj Patel: Thanks Maya. We're mainly trying to understand how Redwood's caching will behave in a multi-tenant environment — our traffic has a heavy tail with lots of repeated system prompts and shared product-level prefixes across customers. We wanna make sure there's no PII leakage and that latency stays within 200 ms p95.
[00:40] Tomás Rivera: Great, yeah — hi all. Quick overview: prefix caching on our side means we materialize the key/value pairs for the prefix tokens in the KV cache so subsequent requests with the same prefix can skip re-encoding and early layers. That reduces both latency and GPU cycles.
[01:05] Leah Kim: Question: what exactly constitutes the cache key? Is it just the raw prompt bytes, or do you canonicalize, include model, model version, tenant id?
[01:20] Tomás: Good question. Our recommended production key is a composite: model name + model_version + canonicalized_prefix_hash + tenant_scope. Canonicalization strips ephemeral ids, normalizes whitespace, and optionally tokenizes to avoid small differences. But we also have a mode where the cache is tenant-agnostic for public shared prompts.
[01:46] Marcus O'Neill: Tenant-agnostic mode sounds risky for us. Our compliance folks will push back unless there's strong isolation. How do you prevent one tenant's prompt from being served to another?
[02:00] Eve Lang: Right, multi-tenant safety is paramount. By default Redwood isolates cache namespaces per account or per-tenant. Shared caches require explicit opt-in and ACLs. For Private/VPC deployments you can choose the namespace mapping — e.g., per-service cluster, per-customer, or even per-route.
[02:22] Sofia Alvarez: And encryption? If the cache store is on a shared cluster, what about KMS/HSM integration and audit logs?
[02:32] Tomás: For hosted we encrypt at rest and integrate with customer-managed keys for enterprise plans. For Redwood Private (on-prem or VPC) the cache lives in customer-controlled storage and uses their KMS. All cache hits/misses are logged — though we do redact token-level content in logs by default.
[02:55] Raj: On hit rates — our ops told us many system-level prefixes repeat across users and that could be a big win. What ranges do you typically see?
[03:05] Tomás: It depends a lot on workload. For chat agents with standardized system prompts we see hit rates anywhere from 20% to 60% on prefix caching, sometimes higher if you aggressively collapse variants. For customer-specific instructions the hit rate is lower. The main lever is key normalization and TTL tuning.
[03:30] Leah: How do you measure hit-rate in a way that's not biased by inference routing (hosted vs dedicated) or load balancers?
[03:39] Tomás: We run traffic replay with a sample of production prompts against the candidate caching policy — synthetic bench. The spreadsheet we'll share has a column for per-prefix frequency, candidate key, and a simulated hit/miss given TTL and eviction policies. It also models batching effects because batching can amplify the benefit if prefixes align within a batch.
[04:05] Maya: Important to note: batching interacts non-trivially with prefix hits. If a cached prefix yields shorter single-request latency but prevents aggregation into larger batches, you might lose throughput efficiency in some setups.
[04:22] Marcus: Can you expand on that? We rely on high throughput at peak times.
[04:28] Tomás: Sure. Two effects: (1) Cached prefixes reduce per-token GPU time, so the runtime will often flush smaller batches faster — which lowers tail latency but might reduce overall GPU occupancy. (2) If you configure batching windows too small, you lose batching benefit; too large, you hurt latency. Our runtime auto-adjusts but the cache can change the latency/throughput sweet spot. We recommend benching with your real request inter-arrival distribution.
[05:00] Leah: How do you handle model variant changes — e.g., quantized vs fp16? Does a cache built on 8-bit quantized kernels transfer to 4-bit quant?
[05:10] Tomás: No, cache compatibility is per-execution/representation. If the kernel changes semantics (quant vs fp), the prefix embeddings/KV values can be incompatible. Our key includes model_variant and quantization_profile. When you change quant settings we mark cache invalidation events. There's a versioned cache metadata header so we can detect mismatches.
[05:40] Raj: So every model update requires a cache warm-up. Any fast warm start strategies?
[05:47] Tomás: Yes. Two strategies: (a) proactive warm-up using a prioritized prefix list pushed to the cache during deploys, and (b) background lazy warm-up where we detect high-frequency prefixes on requests and asynchronously populate the cache. For mission-critical prefixes we push to cache from the client side via a warm-up API.
[06:10] Sofia: About eviction and TTL — what's typical? LRU, LFU, time-based?
[06:17] Tomás: We support LRU and a hybrid LFU+TTL. Most customers use a TTL of 1-24 hours for system prompts and shorter for user-specific content. The cache store also has a size quota per-tenant to avoid noisy neighbors. For Dedicated/Private you can map sizes to GPU pools.
[06:40] Leah: Do you shard cache entries by model/shard id? We run multiple model shards and would like locality to GPU to avoid cross-node network hops.
[06:50] Tomás: Yes, cache sharding can be co-located with model shards. The runtime has a routing table so keys map to node-local KV shards based on a consistent hash. That minimizes network fetches and keeps tail latency low.
[07:05] Marcus: If a cache miss needs remote fetch it could add 50-150 ms, right? How do you bound that?
[07:12] Tomás: Correct; remote warm-up reads can add latency. We mitigate with local SSD caches and prefetch windows. Also, the runtime uses an optimistic path: if KV not found, it begins token generation for the request while the async background populates. That avoids blocking but might duplicate work occasionally.
[07:36] Raj: Are there measurement hooks we can export into our prometheus stack?
[07:40] Eve: Yes, per-route metrics include cache_hits, cache_misses, cache_latency_ms, and prefix_evictions. For Dedicated/Private we can expose these to your Prometheus via pushgateway or direct scrape if network permits.
[07:55] Leah: On the subject of safety, if we canonicalize prompts we might accidentally collapse two distinct prompts that differ in user id placeholders, causing data leakage. How do you prevent that?
[08:05] Tomás: Canonicalization rules are configurable — we provide a library with safe templates and an allowlist/denylist for tokens to remove. For any fields flagged as PII, we keep tenant-scoped namespace or require token redaction. We never canonicalize across tenant boundaries unless explicitly configured.
[08:28] Sofia: We need auditability. If something is served from cache, can you show the original prefix hash and the mapping in audit logs?
[08:36] Tomás: Yes, audit logs include cache_key_hash, model_variant, tenant_id (or tenant_namespace if masked), and hit/miss. We redact raw prompt text in logs for security but keep hashes so you can verify mappings offline.
[08:55] Raj: Let's talk numbers — what perf uplift should we expect for our use-case? We have a mix: 40% system prompts, 50% user messages, 10% long-form generation.
[09:07] Tomás: With 40% stable system prompts, conservative estimate is 25-35% token cost reduction and maybe 20-30% p95 latency improvement for interactive flows. For long-form generation benefits are smaller since the prefix is amortized over many tokens. Our bench will simulate your ratio to give a better estimate.
[09:30] Maya: Reminder: quantization also affects memory pressure — smaller quant means more entries fit in GPU memory so cache hit ratio improves. But as Tomás said, you must treat quant variants as separate cache domains.
[09:46] Leah: Regarding pilot: can we test both Redwood Dedicated and Redwood Private (VPC) to see differences in hit latency and eviction behavior?
[09:54] Tomás: Absolutely. For Dedicated we'll spin a reserved GPU pool with our standard cache sharding. For Private/VPC we'll deploy the cache alongside your infra; that typically improves hit latency because network hops are minimized and you control storage.
[10:12] Marcus: For Private, do you support Ceph/S3-compatible backends?
[10:16] Eve: Yes, we support S3-compatible object stores for cold caches, and local RocksDB/LMDB for hot caches. You can layer them — hot local store + cold S3.
[10:28] Raj: Any gotchas around autoscaling? If autoscaler brings up new worker nodes, how does the cache warm on new nodes?
[10:35] Tomás: New nodes start empty; we rely on cross-node warmup strategies: background population from central orchestrator, proactive warm-up list, and also selective prefetch based on hot keys. There's a brief warm period where misses are higher; we instrument and can route traffic to warmed nodes if needed.
[10:58] Leah: On cost modeling — is there a simple formula we can use to estimate token cost reduction vs added infra cost for Dedicated?
[11:06] Tomás: In the benchmark spreadsheet we include simple TCO rows: baseline tokens * token_cost_hosted vs cached_tokens * adjusted_compute_cost + cache infra. We model GPU-hours saved vs added storage/ops cost. Usually payback in weeks for high-reuse workloads.
[11:26] Sofia: Security question: if we keep token-level redaction, how do you validate correctness of redaction? Could hashed keys leak reconstructed prompts?
[11:36] Tomás: We don't store plaintext in central logs; hashes are salted with tenant-specific salts and we support rotating salts. Reconstruction from salted hashes is computationally infeasible. For compliance we can deploy HSM-backed hashing if needed.
[11:54] Raj: Excellent. A couple last implementation details: do you expose a cache-control header per-request so we can opt-out certain calls?
[11:59] Eve: Yes, you can set cache-control flags at the route level or per-request: no-cache, force-refresh, ttl override. We also have a header to indicate warm-up intent so your front-end can prime entries.
[12:14] Leah: Any limitations with function calling or tool-invocation outputs? Those responses are deterministic for a prefix but include dynamic data sometimes.
[12:23] Tomás: Function/tool output that is deterministic for a given prefix can be cached, but if the tool response includes time-sensitive or user-specific data we recommend no-cache for that route. We provide a way to tag tokens as non-cacheable in the generation graph.
[12:42] Raj: Okay, sounds good. We'll prepare the sample dataset and send over. For pilot success criteria: 30% reduction in token compute and p95 latency under 200 ms for interactive routes.
[12:55] Maya: Noted. We'll run the bench and return results, plus recommended cache key policy for Helix.
[13:03] Marcus: One more thing — reconciliation: if an eviction causes degraded results in production, any fallback policy?
[13:09] Tomás: We have automatic model fallback and can route to a slightly larger model variant or to a stateless path. You can also configure automatic on-miss re-try window. For high-availability, we recommend a small hot cache replicated across nodes.
[13:26] Leah: Sounds good. Thanks everyone.
[13:30] Maya: Thanks all, we'll follow up with the doc and bench spreadsheet.
